title: What Is the Difference Between Law and Gospel?
subtitle: A guide to the distinction between law and gospel in Scripture, why command and promise must not be confused, how the law drives us to Christ, and how rightly dividing the word keeps preaching from moralism

sections.title: Two Words, Not One
sections.body:
There are two words running through the whole Bible, and if you cannot tell them apart you will misread almost every page. One word commands. Do this. Be holy. Love your neighbor. The other word announces. It is finished. Christ died for the ungodly. Your sins are forgiven.

The first is law. The second is gospel. They are not enemies, but they do different work, and confusing them wrecks both.

Law tells you what God requires. Gospel tells you what God has done. Law shows you the standard and exposes your failure to meet it. Gospel announces that Christ met it for you and bore your failure on the cross. The old teachers said the difference between law and gospel is the difference between work and gift, between demand and promise. Lose the distinction and you will turn the gospel into a new set of rules, or the law into something soft and optional. Hold the distinction and the whole Bible comes into focus.

sections.title: What the Law Was Sent to Do
sections.body:
The law is holy, righteous, and good, and it has a job. Its job is to show you the height of God's standard and the depth of your shortfall. It is a mirror. You look into it expecting to see a decent person and you see a sinner.

The law was never given as a ladder you could climb up to God. It was given to show you that you cannot climb at all.

This is what Paul means when he says the law was our tutor to lead us to Christ. Through the law comes the knowledge of sin. The commandment that promised life proved death to me, he writes, because it exposed the rebellion in my own heart. The law does its kindest work when it crushes your confidence in yourself, because only the crushed go looking for a savior. A man who thinks he is keeping the law has not understood it. The law that does its full work leaves you with empty hands, which is exactly where the gospel finds you.

sections.title: What the Gospel Announces
sections.body:
Into those empty hands the gospel speaks an entirely different word. Not do, but done. Not climb, but be carried. The gospel is news, not advice. It reports an event that happened outside of you, in history, on a hill, in a borrowed tomb, before you did anything at all.

Christ kept the law you broke and bore the curse you earned, and in him God credits his obedience to your account as a free gift.

This is why the gospel can be received only by faith and never by effort. The moment you try to earn it, you have turned it back into law. The good news is that God justifies the ungodly, not the improved. He saves sinners, not those who have made themselves a little more presentable first. When the law has stripped you bare, the gospel clothes you in a righteousness that is not your own. That is the gift at the center of the Bible. Anything you add to it as a condition you have to meet, you subtract from it as gospel.

sections.title: Rightly Dividing the Word
sections.body:
Paul tells Timothy to rightly handle the word of truth, and a large part of that skill is knowing, in any given text, whether God is commanding or promising. The same Bible does both, sometimes in the same paragraph, and you have to discern which is which.

Give a frightened, broken sinner more law and you bury him. Give a proud, comfortable sinner cheap comfort and you flatter him to death.

The skill is to read the room and read the text together. To the man crushed by his failure, you do not pile on more commands. You preach Christ crucified and let the gospel raise him. To the man secure in his own goodness, you do not hand him assurance. You let the law do its searching work until he sees his need. A preacher who only ever thunders law produces despair or hypocrites. A preacher who only ever murmurs grace produces people who never feel the weight of sin and so never treasure the cross. Both words, in their right order, for the right person. That is the art.

sections.title: The Law After Grace
sections.body:
Here is where the careful reader avoids a trap. To say the gospel saves us, not the law, is not to throw the law away once we are saved. The law still has a place in the Christian life, no longer as a way to earn God's favor, but as a guide to please the God who already favors us.

The believer keeps the commandments now not to be loved, but because he is loved.

This is the difference between law as taskmaster and law as the household rule of a family already adopted. The same command sounds like crushing demand to the man trying to earn his way in, and like a loving father's instruction to the child already home. The order is everything. Grace first, then obedience as the response to grace. Get that order backward and you have legalism. Keep it and you have a free, glad obedience that flows from gratitude. The law guides the Christian. The gospel saves him. Never let the guide become the savior again.

sections.title: The Word That Saves Is Not the Word That Commands
sections.body:
So read your Bible asking, of each passage, what kind of word this is. Is God showing me his standard, or announcing his rescue. Is this a demand to drive me to Christ, or a promise to give me Christ.

We are saved by the word that announces, never by the word that commands. Confuse the two and you lose the gospel itself.

I have stood in a pulpit and preached law to people who needed the gospel, and watched them leave heavier than they came, and I had to repent of it. The deadliest sermons in the world are the ones that sound religious and never get to grace. The law was given to send you to Christ. The gospel was given to hold you there. Learn to tell them apart, preach them in their order, and you will hand your people the one thing that can save them. Not better advice. Better news, about a finished work, received with empty hands.
